design_detail: Parallel-group randomized clinical trial (MUSIK; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04701866), Montreal, January 2021 to August 2022, reported as a 4-page research letter. 32 patients with treatment-resistant unipolar or bipolar depression who had been accepted for a clinical course of intravenous ketamine were randomized 1:1 to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (15) or usual care without music (17), over 6 infusions in 4 weeks. Primary outcome: change in systolic blood pressure from the start of each infusion to its end at 40 minutes, analysed across all infusions with generalized estimating equations; secondary outcomes are to be reported elsewhere.
can_establish: That in patients receiving clinical intravenous ketamine infusions for treatment-resistant depression, curated music during the infusion was followed by a smaller rise in systolic blood pressure over the infusion than usual care without music (about 7 mm Hg less), with randomization protecting the comparison from confounding.
cannot_establish: Whether the smaller rise matters clinically (how many patients in each arm needed blood-pressure treatment is not reported); what music did to depression, dissociation or the experience (deferred to later papers); whether the effect comes from the music itself rather than from headphones, attention or expectation (the control was no music, with no sound or attention control); or anything about ketamine taken outside supervised clinical infusions.

sample.recruitment: Patients assessed for a clinical course of intravenous ketamine: 40 assessed, 8 excluded (2 active substance use disorder, 4 depressive episodes not meeting resistance criteria, 2 declined), and all 32 remaining patients randomized (Figure 1, p. 2). Clinical sample, Montreal; ethics approval from the Douglas Mental Health University Institute and the Jewish General Hospital (p. 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Current unipolar or bipolar depressive episode refractory to at least 2 adequate medication trials, accepted for treatment with intravenous ketamine, written informed consent; full criteria are in the protocol supplement, which was not read (p. 1, Methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: 23 of 32 (72%) women; mean age 45.9 years (SD 14.2); self-reported race 27 White (84%), 2 Hispanic, 1 Asian, 1 Black, 1 Middle Eastern (p. 2). Baseline characteristics by arm are in eTable 1 of a supplement that was not read.
sample.attrition: Music arm: 1 lost to 8-week follow-up, 1 excluded from the study for violating the clinic's safety protocol, 1 did not complete the treatment course. Usual care: 1 lost to follow-up, 3 discontinued (1 chose to receive music, 1 because of psychoactive effects, 1 because illness symptoms worsened), 1 excluded from analysis without a stated reason. 28 completed per protocol; 181 infusions were given out of a possible 192 (editors' arithmetic: 87 of 90 with music, 94 of 102 without) (Figure 1, p. 2; Results, p. 3).
sample.selection_effects: People already accepted for clinical ketamine treatment, mostly White women in mid-life, in one city; active substance use disorder excluded. Small sample (the sample-size calculation asked for 30).

exposure.measurement: Assigned intervention: curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion (playlists in eTable 2, not read) versus usual care without music (p. 1, Methods, 2nd paragraph). How the music was delivered (headphones or speakers) is not described in the letter.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Clinical treatment conditions given in hospital, not patterns of use: six intravenous subanaesthetic ketamine infusions of 0.5 mg/kg, each over 40 minutes, across 4 weeks (p. 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Active substance use disorder excluded at screening; concurrent medicines, including antidepressants or antihypertensives, are not reported in the letter.

comparison.controls: Usual care: the same clinical infusions without music (17 randomized).
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1; baseline characteristics by arm are not shown in the letter (eTable 1 not read). Raw mean systolic pressure at the start of infusions was similar in both arms, about 119–120 mm Hg (Figure 2B, read from the figure).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; baseline hypertension and use of antihypertensive medicines by arm are not reported in the letter.

outcomes.instruments: Blood pressure: the mean of three measurements immediately before the infusion (0 minutes) and at its end (40 minutes); the device and who took the measurements are not described in the letter (p. 1, Methods, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: change in systolic blood pressure from 0 to 40 minutes of each infusion; 40 minutes was chosen in advance as the time of peak plasma concentrations (p. 1). Diastolic change is reported alongside.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; patients and staff necessarily knew the allocation.

analysis.effect_sizes: Population-averaged effect of music across 181 infusions (generalized estimating equations): systolic change β = −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008; diastolic change β = −0.8 mm Hg (95% CI printed as −1.59 to 3.18), P = .58 (p. 3). Read from Figure 2A (approximate): mean systolic rise about 11.5 mm Hg with music and about 18.5 mm Hg without; diastolic rise about 7.5 and 8 mm Hg. Figure 2B (approximate): raw mean systolic about 119–120 mm Hg at the start in both arms and about 131 vs 138 mm Hg at 40 minutes (p. 2).
analysis.covariates: Not described in the letter; the model accounts for repeated infusions within patients, with inverse-probability weighting for missing data (p. 1, Methods, 4th paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04701866; the letter says the 40-minute time point was chosen prospectively and provides the protocol and statistical analysis plan as Supplement 1. Neither the registry record nor the supplement was read, so the registered primary outcome and analysis were not compared with the report.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only blood pressure is reported; all secondary outcomes, including depression outcomes, are deferred to later publications (p. 3, Discussion, 1st paragraph).
analysis.power: The sample-size calculation (in the supplementary methods, not read) estimated 30 patients to be sufficient; 32 were randomized (p. 1).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 32 randomized patients receiving clinical intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression, systolic blood pressure rose about 7 mm Hg less over infusions with music than without (β −7.4 mm Hg, 95% CI −12.0 to −2.9); diastolic pressure did not differ detectably.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion calls music a "feasible, benign, nonpharmacological approach" to improving the haemodynamic response to ketamine (p. 3). 'Benign' rests only on no serious adverse events being recorded, and 'improving' is not tied to any clinical outcome: the introduction says up to 20% of patients on intravenous ketamine need medication for treatment-induced hypertension, but the letter does not report how many patients in each arm did. The suggestion that ketamine's psychoactive effects may amplify the effects of music and the environment (p. 3) is not tested here, since no psychoactive or experience measures are reported. The authors acknowledge the modest sample.

timeline.event: Bradt and Dileo, Cochrane review of music interventions for mechanically ventilated patients, cited as background that music improves the haemodynamic response to other medical interventions (p. 1, reference 2).
Kheirkhah et al., scoping review of music and response to ketamine or esketamine, on the project's reading list; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial; the letter cites no earlier study of music and ketamine's blood-pressure effects, and its secondary outcomes had not been seen by this reader. No replication is known from the papers read here.

funding.funder: Réseau québécois sur le suicide, les troubles de l'humeur et les troubles associés (RQSHA); the funder had no role in design, conduct, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing, review or the decision to submit (p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr Beaulieu: grants from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and from Otsuka-Lundbeck (investigator-initiated trial); personal fees from Abbvie, Otsuka, Janssen and Sunovion (consultant and speaker) and from Takeda, Idorsia and Eisai (consultant), outside the submitted work. Dr Rej: clinician-scientist salary award from Fonds de Recherche Santé Québec, grants from Mitacs, shareholder of Aifred Health, and member of a steering committee for an AbbVie post-observational marketing study, outside the submitted work. Dr Richard-Devantoy: grants from the RQSHA during the study. No other disclosures (pp. 3–4).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, McGill University; Lady Davis Institute, Jewish General Hospital; Douglas Mental Health University Institute and McGill Group for Suicide Studies, Montreal. No disclosed interest in music products or playlists. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A larger multi-site randomized trial of music versus a sound or attention control (for example headphones with silence or neutral sound) during clinical ketamine infusions, with automated or blinded blood-pressure measurement and clinically relevant outcomes (pressure above treatment thresholds, need for antihypertensive treatment), reported together with dissociation, experience and depression outcomes.

domains.note: 1:1 random assignment is stated, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described in the letter and the baseline table by arm is in a supplement that was not read; starting systolic pressure was similar in both arms (Figure 2B).

Open-label by necessity. One usual-care patient chose to receive music and one music patient was excluded for a safety-protocol violation; the analysis is described as intention-to-treat with inverse-probability weighting, yet one usual-care patient was excluded from analysis without a stated reason.

181 of a possible 192 infusions (94%); more were missing without music (8 vs 3), including drop-outs for psychoactive effects and worsening illness; inverse-probability weighting was used, with its assumptions not described in the letter.
Blood pressure is objective and averaged over three readings, but the device and whether the person measuring knew the allocation are not described in the letter.
Registered, with the 40-minute time point stated as chosen in advance, but the registry record and the analysis plan were not read for this card; other outcomes are deferred.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small randomized trial with an objective primary outcome and an intention-to-treat analysis across repeated infusions; the uncertainties are details not given in the letter (concealment, how blood pressure was measured, baseline balance in a supplement not read), an unexplained exclusion from analysis, and more missing infusions in the usual-care arm. Cite it for: curated music during clinical intravenous ketamine infusions for treatment-resistant depression was followed by a smaller systolic rise (about 7 mm Hg) than no music. Do not cite it for clinical benefit, for effects on mood, dissociation or experience, or for any use outside supervised clinical infusions.

key_findings.finding: MUSIK randomized trial (NCT04701866), Montreal, January 2021 to August 2022: patients with a unipolar or bipolar depressive episode refractory to at least 2 adequate medication trials, accepted for intravenous ketamine, were randomized 1:1 to curated music throughout each 40-minute infusion or usual care without music, over a course of 6 infusions of 0.5 mg/kg in 4 weeks.

Primary outcome: change in systolic blood pressure between the mean of three readings at 0 and at 40 minutes of each infusion, 40 minutes having been chosen in advance as the time of peak plasma values; analysed with generalized estimating equations across all 6 infusions, intention-to-treat with inverse-probability weighting for missing data; 30 patients estimated to be sufficient.
32 patients randomized (15 music, 17 usual care): 23 (72%) women, mean age 45.9 (SD 14.2), 27 (84%) White; no serious adverse events were recorded; 28 completed the trial per protocol.

Across 181 infusions (87 with music, 94 without), music reduced the rise in systolic blood pressure from the start to the end of the infusion: β = −7.4 mm Hg (95% CI −12.0 to −2.9), P = .008. Diastolic blood pressure did not differ detectably: β = −0.8 mm Hg, P = .58.
key_findings.note: The printed diastolic interval (−1.59 to 3.18) is centred on +0.8, not −0.8 (see reporting issues). Editors' calculation: the systolic interval implies a Wald z of about 3.2 (p about 0.001), smaller than the printed P = .008.

key_findings.finding: Figure 2, read approximately from the bars and points: the mean systolic rise over the infusion was about 11.5 mm Hg with music and about 18.5 mm Hg without; diastolic rises were about 7.5 and 8 mm Hg. Raw mean systolic pressure started at about 119–120 mm Hg in both arms and reached about 131 mm Hg with music and 138 mm Hg without at 40 minutes.
key_findings.note: Values read from the figure on a 300-dpi crop; approximate.

key_findings.finding: Flow: of 40 patients assessed for ketamine treatment, 8 were excluded (2 active substance use disorder, 4 not meeting resistance criteria, 2 declined); in usual care 3 discontinued (1 chose to receive music, 1 because of psychoactive effects, 1 because illness worsened) and 1 was excluded from analysis; in the music arm 1 was excluded from the study for a safety-protocol violation; 1 per arm was lost to 8-week follow-up.

Background stated by the authors: up to 20% of patients receiving intravenous ketamine for treatment-resistant depression need medication for treatment-induced hypertension (cited from McIntyre et al., 2021).
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure; the trial does not report how many patients in each arm needed such treatment.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that music decreased ketamine-induced systolic changes and may be a feasible, benign, non-drug way to improve the haemodynamic response; secondary trial outcomes are to be published elsewhere; they suggest ketamine's psychoactive effects may amplify the effects of music and environment, and name the modest sample as a limitation.

reporting_issues.issue: The diastolic estimate is printed as β = −0.8 mm Hg with a 95% CI of −1.59 to 3.18, an interval centred on +0.8; a symmetric interval around −0.8 with the same width would be −3.18 to 1.59. Figure 2A shows a slightly smaller diastolic rise with music, consistent with the negative estimate.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval's signs appear transposed (editors' arithmetic); the conclusion of no detectable diastolic difference is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: For systolic pressure, the printed interval (−12.0 to −2.9) implies a standard error of about 2.3 mm Hg and a Wald p of about 0.001, while P = .008 is printed (editors' calculation); the diastolic P (.58) is likewise larger than its interval implies (about 0.51).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the method behind the P values is in a supplement not read. Both versions indicate a systolic difference unlikely under no effect.

reporting_issues.issue: In the flow diagram, the usual-care box beside the music arm's 15 analysed for the primary outcome reads 16 analysed for secondary outcome measures with 1 excluded from analysis, so the number analysed for the primary outcome in usual care is not stated explicitly, and an exclusion from analysis sits uneasily with the stated intention-to-treat approach; no reason is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The primary analysis apparently used 31 of 32 randomized patients (15 + 16, editors' inference).

reporting_issues.issue: The article information gives the acceptance date as December 13, 2022, but the Methods say the analyses were conducted from September 2022 to July 2023, and the article was published on February 5, 2024.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the dates is probably wrong (an acceptance in December 2023 would fit); no effect on the results.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Greenway_2024_MusicKetamineRCT.pdf, version of record (JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(2):e2354719, reprinted), 4 pages printed 1/4 to 4/4, all read: Introduction, Methods, Results, Figure 1 (flow) and Figure 2 (checked on the rendered page and a 300-dpi crop), Discussion, article information, conflicts, funding, registration and references. Not read: Supplement 1 (protocol and statistical analysis plan), Supplement 2 (eMethods, eTable 1 baseline characteristics, eTable 2 playlists), Supplement 3, and the ClinicalTrials.gov record, none of which was among the files.
